It requires finding the amplitude and minimum, building a cosine model with a phase shift from the max location, evaluating at a special angle (pi/2), and solving cos(theta)=1/2 for two solutions in one period. Each step is standard in scope and uses exact unit-circle values with no calculator. Difficulty comes from sequencing several routine skills, which fits a full-mock exam item rather than a single-concept basic item. Nothing is hard because of unfair sources.

payload.title: Body temperature modeled by a sinusoidal function

stimulus.description: A person's body temperature $T(t)$, in degrees Fahrenheit, is modeled by a sinusoidal function of $t$, the number of hours after midnight. The highest temperature, $98.8^\circ$F, occurs at $t=18$ hours, and the period is $24$ hours. The midline value is $98^\circ$F. No calculator is allowed.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Find the amplitude of $T$ and the lowest temperature of the model.

rubric_rows.criterion: Amplitude and lowest temperature values

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Write an expression for $T(t)$ in the form $T(t)=a\cos(b(t-c))+d$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Expression with the amplitude and the midline value
Expression with b = pi over 12 and the shift c
alt_solutions: an equivalent sine form with a different shift

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Find the temperature at $t=24$ hours.

rubric_rows.criterion: Value with units

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Find the two times in the first 24 hours after midnight at which the temperature is $98.4^\circ$F.

rubric_rows.criterion: Equation setting the cosine factor equal to one half
Both time values

The scope fits 3.7 with 3.5 and 3.6, and the rubric rows are consistent, with valid alternatives noted for part B. Minor weaknesses: common_errors are empty, and the 'no calculator' sentence in the stimulus is redundant.
